quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the ideas behind a product-mix decision: scarce resources, constraints, contribution per frame and feasibility.

questions.q: In the yarn-mix problem, which resource is described as scarce?
questions.explain: The mill has only 46 frames; every count competes for them. Cotton is treated as a variable cost that can be bought as needed.

questions.q: What are the two constraints in the lecture's plan?
options: 46 frames and Rs 644,000 of fixed cost
46 frames and 780 bags of daily shipment
questions.explain: A plan is feasible only if the frames allotted total no more than 46 and the bags produced total no more than 780 a day. Fixed cost is a given, not a limit.

questions.q: Coarser counts earn more contribution per bag than finer counts.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: Ne 6 earns Rs 879 per bag and Ne 20 earns Rs 1,694. Coarse counts win on bags per frame, not on contribution per bag.

questions.q: Why does a coarse count such as Ne 6 produce more bags per frame per day than Ne 20?
options: A coarse yarn delivers far more weight per spindle per shift at normal spindle speeds
questions.explain: Ounces per spindle per shift (OPS) are much higher for coarse yarn, so 25.65 bags come off a Ne 6 frame against 9.27 from a Ne 20 frame.

questions.q: When only the frames are limiting, the count to favour is the one with the highest…
questions.explain: The scarce resource should earn the most per unit of itself. Contribution per bag ignores how many bags a frame makes; bags per frame ignores what each bag earns.

questions.q: Which count has the highest contribution per frame per day in the lecture's table?
questions.explain: Ne 8 earns about Rs 23,750 per frame per day, slightly ahead of Ne 10 (Rs 22,786) and Ne 6 (Rs 22,553). Ne 20 is lowest at Rs 15,703 despite the highest contribution per bag.

questions.q: A plan that uses only 36 of the 46 frames is feasible but leaves capacity idle.
questions.explain: The lecture's starting plan of six frames per count uses 36 frames and ships 632 bags: within both limits, but ten frames and the fixed cost they carry earn nothing.

questions.q: The phrase "the shipping limit binds" means…
options: the plan ships fewer than 780 bags
the best plan would ship more than 780 bags if it could, so the limit is what stops it
questions.explain: A binding constraint is one that the optimal plan uses fully. Running every frame on coarse counts would exceed 780 bags, so the shipping limit, not the frame count alone, shapes the answer.

questions.q: The lecture calls the worksheet a "hand-driven linear programme". What does that mean?
options: You try allocations yourself until the totals meet both limits and contribution is highest
The sheet draws a line graph
questions.explain: A linear programme maximises a linear objective (contribution) under linear constraints (frames, bags). Here the student does the search by editing row 2 instead of using a solver.

questions.q: Fixed cost in this lecture is charged for…
options: all 46 frames, whether running or not
questions.explain: Row 13 shows 46 × Rs 14,000 = Rs 644,000 regardless of the 36 frames allotted. Idle frames still carry depreciation, finance and labour.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How each row of the yarn-mix sheet is built and how the totals respond when frames, prices or limits change.

questions.q: Contribution per bag for a count is…
options: price per bag − variable cost per bag excl. EDS − export development surcharge
price per bag − fixed cost per frame
price per bag × bags per frame
questions.explain: For Ne 6: 5,445 − 4,552 − 13.61 = Rs 879. Fixed cost is never deducted per bag in a contribution analysis.

questions.q: Contribution per frame per day equals…
options: contribution per bag ÷ bags per frame per day
contribution per bag × bags per frame per day
questions.explain: Ne 20: Rs 1,694 × 9.27 bags = Rs 15,703 per frame per day. Multiplying by frames allotted instead gives the total for that count, not the per-frame figure.

questions.q: Total bags per day for a count is…
options: bags per frame per day ÷ frames allotted
bags per frame per day × frames allotted
questions.explain: Six frames × 25.65 bags = 153.9 bags of Ne 6 a day. Summed across the counts it must stay at or below 780.

questions.q: Profit per day = total contribution per day − 46 × Rs 14,000.
questions.explain: Rs 729,021 − Rs 644,000 = Rs 85,021 in the lecture's starting plan.

questions.q: If one more frame is moved from Ne 6 to Ne 8, what happens to the two totals?
options: Bags fall by 2.25 and contribution rises by about Rs 1,200
Bags rise by 2.25 and contribution falls
Bags fall by 25.65 and contribution falls by Rs 22,553
questions.explain: Bags per frame drop from 25.65 to 23.40 (−2.25) while contribution per frame rises from Rs 22,553 to Rs 23,752 (+Rs 1,199). The frame total is unchanged.

questions.q: Bags per frame per day in the sheet is OPS × 0.9. If efficiency improves so the factor becomes 0.95, which figures change?
options: Bags per frame per day, total bags and contribution per frame for every count
questions.explain: More bags per frame means more contribution per frame and more bags against the 780 limit; price and fixed cost are untouched.

questions.q: Why does the export development surcharge differ between counts in row 9?
options: It is a fixed Rs 13.61 for every count
It is 0.25 % of price per bag, and prices differ by count
It depends on bags per frame
questions.explain: 0.25 % × Rs 5,445 = Rs 13.61 for Ne 6 but 0.25 % × Rs 6,261 = Rs 15.65 for Ne 20. The variable cost excluding surcharge is the same Rs 4,552 for all.

questions.q: Which statement about the direction of effect is correct?
options: Raising the price of Ne 20 raises its contribution per frame by 9.27 × (price rise less surcharge)
Raising the price of Ne 20 raises its bags per frame
Raising the price of Ne 20 changes the contribution of Ne 6
Raising the price of Ne 20 lowers fixed cost
questions.explain: Each extra rupee of price adds Rs 0.9975 to contribution per bag (after the 0.25 % surcharge), and the frame makes 9.27 bags. Other counts and fixed cost are independent.

questions.q: If the shipping limit were removed, the best plan would put all 46 frames on the count with the highest contribution per frame per day.
questions.explain: With only the frame constraint, contribution per frame is the sole criterion: 46 frames on Ne 8 would earn about 46 × Rs 23,752 ≈ Rs 1,092,600 a day (but ship about 1,076 bags).

questions.q: Profit per month in the sheet is found by…
questions.explain: Rs 85,021 × 30 ≈ Rs 2,550,600 a month. Multiplying contribution rather than profit would omit the fixed cost.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute contributions, bag totals and feasibility for plans using the lecture's six counts.

questions.q: Ne 12 sells at Rs 5,853 per bag; variable cost excluding surcharge is Rs 4,552 and the surcharge is 0.25 % of price. What is the contribution per bag, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: Surcharge = 5,853 × 0.0025 = Rs 14.63; contribution = 5,853 − 4,552 − 14.63 = Rs 1,286 (the sheet rounds to 1,287).

questions.q: Ne 10 earns Rs 1,151 per bag and a frame makes 19.80 bags a day. What is the contribution per frame per day?
questions.explain: Rs 1,151 × 19.80 = Rs 22,790 (Rs 22,786 in the sheet using unrounded contribution).

questions.q: Six frames are allotted to each of the six counts. Bags per frame per day are 25.65, 23.40, 19.80, 15.30, 11.97 and 9.27. How many bags a day does the mill produce in total (to one decimal)?
questions.explain: 6 × 105.39 = 632.3 bags, within the 780 limit.

questions.q: The six-frames-each plan earns a total contribution of Rs 729,021 a day. Fixed cost is 46 frames × Rs 14,000. What is the profit per day?
If all 46 frames ran Ne 8 at 23.40 bags per frame per day, how many bags would be produced a day?
questions.explain: 46 × 23.40 = 1,076.4 bags, far above the 780 bags that can be shipped, so this plan is infeasible.

questions.q: A plan puts x frames on Ne 10 (19.80 bags per frame) and the rest of 46 on Ne 20 (9.27 bags per frame) so that exactly 780 bags are made. Find x to one decimal place.
With 33.6 frames on Ne 10 at Rs 22,786 per frame per day and 12.4 frames on Ne 20 at Rs 15,703, what is the total contribution per day, to the nearest thousand rupees?
The optimal plan earns a contribution of about Rs 960,000 a day against fixed cost of Rs 644,000. What is the profit per day?
questions.explain: Rs 960,000 − Rs 644,000 = Rs 316,000 a day, nearly four times the Rs 85,000 of the six-frames-each plan.

questions.q: All 46 frames on Ne 12 (15.30 bags per frame, Rs 19,685 per frame per day). Is the plan feasible, and what does it earn?
questions.explain: 46 × 15.30 = 703.8 bags, under 780, and 46 × 19,685 = Rs 905,510. Feasible but about Rs 55,000 a day below the Ne 10 + Ne 20 mix.

questions.q: Ne 20 sells at Rs 6,261 per bag and Ne 6 at Rs 5,445. By how many rupees per bag does the Ne 20 price exceed Ne 6?
questions.explain: Rs 6,261 − Rs 5,445 = Rs 816 per bag, which is also (apart from a Rs 2 surcharge difference) the gap in contribution per bag: Rs 1,694 − Rs 879 = Rs 815.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning decisions in a spinning mill: which frames to switch, how to respond to new limits and what to tell the marketing team.

questions.q: The port can suddenly handle 900 bags a day instead of 780. How should the plan change?
options: No change; frames are the only limit
Shift frames towards coarser counts, since more bags can now be shipped and coarse counts earn more per frame
questions.explain: The shipping limit was binding. Loosening it lets the mill move towards Ne 8 and Ne 10, the counts with the highest contribution per frame, which it had to ration for their high bag output.

questions.q: A merchant offers a large order for Ne 20 at Rs 6,261 per bag. The production manager wants to accept because it has the highest contribution per bag. What is the right response?
options: Accept all of it: highest contribution per bag is what matters
Point out that Ne 20 earns the least per frame (Rs 15,703) and should only take frames the shipping limit forces away from coarser counts
Accept only if the surcharge is waived
questions.explain: A frame on Ne 20 earns Rs 15,703 a day, a frame on Ne 8 Rs 23,752. Ne 20 is used in the optimum only because its low bag output keeps shipments within 780.

questions.q: If a seventh count with contribution per frame of Rs 25,000 and 30 bags per frame per day became available, it would always be better to put all frames on it.
questions.explain: 46 × 30 = 1,380 bags, far beyond the shipping limit. It would displace some coarse counts, but the plan would still have to mix with finer counts to stay within 780 bags.

questions.q: Fixed cost per frame rises from Rs 14,000 to Rs 16,000 a day. What happens to the optimal mix?
options: The mix shifts to finer counts
The mix shifts to coarser counts
The mix is unchanged; only the profit falls by Rs 92,000 a day
The mill should run fewer frames
questions.explain: Fixed cost does not depend on the count chosen, so it cannot change which allocation maximises contribution. Profit falls by 46 × Rs 2,000 = Rs 92,000 a day.

questions.q: The marketing team can raise the price of Ne 10 by Rs 100 per bag or the price of Ne 20 by Rs 200 per bag, but not both. In the optimal plan (33.6 frames Ne 10, 12.4 frames Ne 20), which is worth more?
options: Ne 10: about Rs 66,500 a day against about Rs 23,000 for Ne 20
questions.explain: Ne 10: 33.6 frames × 19.8 bags × Rs 100 × 0.9975 ≈ Rs 66,400. Ne 20: 12.4 × 9.27 × Rs 200 × 0.9975 ≈ Rs 22,900. More bags make the smaller rise worth more.

questions.q: A planner proposes 20 frames on Ne 6 and 26 on Ne 20. Check feasibility.
questions.explain: 20 × 25.65 = 513 bags plus 26 × 9.27 = 241 bags = 754 bags, within 780, and 46 frames exactly. Feasible, though it earns less than the Ne 10 + Ne 20 mix.

questions.q: Cotton prices push the variable cost per bag up by Rs 100 for every count. Which count's contribution per frame per day falls the most?
options: Ne 20, because it has the highest price
Ne 6, because it makes the most bags per frame
All counts fall equally by Rs 100
questions.explain: Contribution per frame falls by Rs 100 × bags per frame: Ne 6 loses 25.65 × 100 = Rs 2,565 a day per frame, Ne 20 only Rs 927. A cost rise per bag hurts coarse counts most, so the mix must be recomputed and the limits re-checked.

questions.q: Leaving ten frames idle, as in the six-frames-each plan, costs the mill about Rs 140,000 a day of fixed cost with nothing earned against it.
questions.explain: 10 × Rs 14,000 = Rs 140,000 a day of depreciation, finance and labour is incurred by frames that earn no contribution. Any count with positive contribution per frame should fill them, subject to the bag limit.

questions.q: The best plan uses fractional frames (33.6 and 12.4). How is this applied in a real mill?
options: Round to whole frames (34 and 12, or 33 and 13) and re-check the bag limit and contribution
Ignore the plan since fractions are impossible
questions.explain: 34 on Ne 10 and 12 on Ne 20 gives 673.2 + 111.2 = 784.4 bags, just over 780; 33 and 13 gives 653.4 + 120.5 = 773.9 bags, feasible. A frame can also change count part-way through a month.

questions.q: Which report would be most useful to management each morning, following this lecture?
options: Contribution per frame per day for each count, with the frame and bag totals against their limits
questions.explain: The decision is driven by contribution per frame and by whether the plan stays within 46 frames and 780 bags; those are the figures that change with prices and OPS.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions on the mix: binding constraints, trade-offs between counts and the slips students make when comparing per-bag and per-frame figures.

questions.q: Moving one frame from Ne 20 (9.27 bags, Rs 15,703 per frame per day) to Ne 10 (19.80 bags, Rs 22,786) adds how many bags per day to shipments?
questions.explain: 19.80 − 9.27 = 10.53 extra bags and Rs 7,083 extra contribution per day. At the 780 limit this is the trade-off the planner faces.

questions.q: At the shipping limit, the useful measure for a bag-limited mill is contribution per bag. Which count is highest on that measure and which is highest per frame?
options: Ne 20 per bag; Ne 8 per frame
Ne 8 per bag; Ne 20 per frame
questions.explain: Rs 1,694 per bag for Ne 20 against Rs 23,752 per frame for Ne 8. The optimum balances the two measures because both limits bind together.

questions.q: A plan of 25 frames on Ne 8 (23.40 bags) and 21 frames on Ne 20 (9.27 bags) is proposed. How many bags a day does it make?
questions.explain: 585.0 + 194.67 = 779.67 bags, just within the limit. Its contribution, 25 × 23,752 + 21 × 15,703 ≈ Rs 923,600, is still below the Ne 10 + Ne 20 plan.

questions.q: Why is the Ne 8 + Ne 20 plan (about Rs 923,600) worse than the Ne 10 + Ne 20 plan (about Rs 960,000) even though Ne 8 has the highest contribution per frame?
options: Because Ne 8 ships too few bags
Because Ne 8's high bag output forces more frames onto low-earning Ne 20 to stay within 780 bags
Because Ne 8 has a higher surcharge
Because Ne 10 has the highest contribution per bag
questions.explain: Each Ne 8 frame uses 23.4 of the 780 bags, so only 25 fit and 21 frames must take Ne 20 at Rs 15,703. Ne 10 uses fewer bags per frame, allowing 33.6 high-earning frames and only 12.4 on Ne 20.

questions.q: Because fixed cost is Rs 644,000 regardless of the plan, the plan that maximises total contribution also maximises profit.
questions.explain: Profit = contribution − a constant. Maximising one maximises the other, which is why the sheet focuses on contribution per frame.

questions.q: The six-frames-each plan ships 632.3 bags and the limit is 780. How many more bags a day could be shipped?
questions.explain: 780 − 632.3 = 147.7 bags of unused shipping capacity, alongside 10 unused frames: the plan is loose on both limits.

questions.q: A student says: "Ne 6 at 25.65 bags × Rs 5,445 = Rs 139,664 per frame per day, so Ne 6 is best." What is wrong?
options: Price, not contribution, has been used; variable cost of Rs 4,552 and the surcharge must be deducted first, leaving Rs 22,553
questions.explain: Revenue per frame means nothing on its own; the frame's earnings are contribution per bag (Rs 879) × 25.65 bags = Rs 22,553.

questions.q: Daily profit of the optimal plan is about Rs 316,000 and of the six-frames-each plan Rs 85,021. What is the monthly gain (30 days) from switching, to the nearest thousand rupees?
questions.explain: Rs 230,979 × 30 ≈ Rs 6,929,000 a month, nearly Rs 7 million from re-allocating the same 46 frames.

questions.q: The exchange rate rises from Rs 60 to Rs 66 per dollar. Prices per bag in rupees rise by 10 % while the Rs 4,552 variable cost is unchanged. Which count's contribution per frame rises most in rupees?
options: Ne 20, because its price is highest
Ne 6, because 25.65 bags × 10 % of Rs 5,445 is the largest per-frame gain
questions.explain: Gain per frame ≈ bags per frame × 10 % of price: Ne 6 gives 25.65 × Rs 544 ≈ Rs 13,900; Ne 20 only 9.27 × Rs 626 ≈ Rs 5,800. A weaker rupee favours the coarse counts.

questions.q: If both limits bind in the optimum, how many counts does the best plan normally use?
questions.explain: A linear programme with two binding constraints has an optimum at a corner where two activities are positive. That is why the lecture's answer uses just Ne 10 and Ne 20.
